title: Pre-Analytical Errors & the Total Testing Process

references.label: WHO Laboratory Quality Management System Handbook
CLSI Standards for Clinical Laboratory Practice

summary: The Total Testing Process (TTP) splits laboratory work into pre-analytical, analytical, and post-analytical phases. The pre-analytical phase — everything from test ordering through specimen arrival at the bench — is where most laboratory errors actually originate.
explanation: Multiple published error-rate studies across clinical laboratories consistently find that the pre-analytical phase (patient/specimen identification, collection, labeling, handling, transport, and processing before testing begins) accounts for the majority of total laboratory errors, far more than the analytical phase itself. Common pre-analytical error types include misidentification, wrong container/anticoagulant, inadequate volume, hemolysis, clotting, delayed transport, and incorrect storage temperature. Because analyzers and trained staff can produce a technically 'correct' result on a compromised specimen, pre-analytical errors are dangerous specifically because they are often invisible downstream — the number that comes out can look plausible while not reflecting the patient. This entry defines the framework; specimen-specific handling rules are covered in the related specimen collection and rejection entries.

commonMisconceptions: Assuming a result is trustworthy simply because the analyzer produced a number — an analyzer cannot detect that a specimen was drawn from the wrong patient or degraded in transit.
